anchorData:
ANCHOR OBJECTS (Lesson 1 collection): (1) aluminium sufuria, Al, Z=13; (2) copper wire in kettle/jiko cable, Cu, Z=29; (3) mabati roof, iron (Fe, Z=26) coated with zinc (Zn, Z=30); (4) table salt, NaCl, Na Z=11, Cl Z=17; (5) Mombasa water treated with chlorine; (6) Thika Road street lamp glowing yellow-orange with sodium vapour. DEMO: a pea-sized piece of sodium (about 0.1 g) is cut under oil, dropped into a trough of water; it floats, fizzes, darts about, melts into a ball, and the solution turns pink with phenolphthalein, showing an alkali (NaOH) forms. Sodium is stored under paraffin oil.

FIRST 20 ELEMENTS (symbol, Z, family): H1 (non-metal, not in any family), He2 noble, Li3 alkali, Be4 alkaline earth, B5, C6, N7, O8 (not in the four families), F9 halogen, Ne10 noble, Na11 alkali, Mg12 alkaline earth, Al13 (other metal, not in the four families), Si14, P15, S16 (other), Cl17 halogen, Ar18 noble, K19 alkali, Ca20 alkaline earth. Transition metals (Sc to Zn, including Fe26, Cu29, Zn30) sit in the block between Group 2 and Group 13 starting from Period 4. Pb (Z=82) is in Group 14 (a post-transition metal) but is taught with the metals in Lesson 7 as 'heavy metals' with transition metals for use comparison.

OUTER ELECTRONS: Group 1 = 1; Group 2 = 2; Group 17 = 7; Group 18 = 8 (He = 2, full first shell). Electron arrangement: Li 2,1; Na 2,8,1; K 2,8,8,1; Mg 2,8,2; Cl 2,8,7; Ne 2,8; Ar 2,8,8.

PHYSICAL DATA (approximate, rounded, secondary data table for Lesson 3): Na: density 0.97 g/cm3, melting 98 C, soft (cut with knife), conducts electricity. K: density 0.86 g/cm3, melting 63 C, soft, conducts. Li: density 0.53 g/cm3, melting 181 C, soft, conducts. Mg: density 1.74 g/cm3, melting 650 C, harder, conducts. Ca: density 1.55 g/cm3, melting 842 C, harder, conducts. Fe: density 7.87 g/cm3, melting 1538 C, hard, conducts. Cu: density 8.96 g/cm3, melting 1085 C, hard, excellent conductor. Zn: density 7.14 g/cm3, melting 420 C, conducts. Al: density 2.70 g/cm3, melting 660 C, conducts. Pb: density 11.34 g/cm3, melting 327 C, soft, heavy, poor-to-moderate conductor. Cl2: greenish-yellow gas, melts at -101 C, boils at -34 C, non-conductor. Ne: colourless gas, boils at -246 C, non-conductor. Ar: colourless gas, boils at -186 C, non-conductor. Checks: Na, K and Li are less dense than water (1.00 g/cm3) so float; Mg, Ca and transition metals are denser than water. Densest in the table: Pb (11.34); lowest melting among metals listed: K (63 C); highest melting: Fe (1538 C).

REACTIVITY ORDER (Lessons 4 to 5): Alkali metals with water: Li slow fizz, Na fast fizz and melts, K very fast and lilac flame. Mg: no visible reaction with cold water; burns in air with a bright white flame forming white MgO; reacts with dilute HCl giving bubbles of H2. Reactivity order: K > Na > Li > Ca > Mg. Sodium is more reactive than magnesium.

KEY EQUATIONS: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2; 4Na + O2 -> 2Na2O; 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO; Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2; 2Li + 2H2O -> 2LiOH + H2; 2K + 2H2O -> 2KOH + H2; 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl; Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2.

WATER TREATMENT (Lesson 6): Chlorine added to water at about 0.5 mg per litre (0.5 mg/L) of free chlorine at the treatment works; it kills bacteria that cause cholera and typhoid. Chlorine gas is toxic at high concentration, so only a small safe dose is used.

TRANSITION METAL USES (Lesson 7): Cu - electrical wire (excellent conductor, ductile); Fe - structural steel and mabati base (strong, cheap); Zn - galvanising coat on mabati (protects iron from rusting by sacrificial protection); Pb - car batteries and radiation shielding (very dense, but toxic, so use is being reduced); Al - sufuria (light, good heat conductor, resists corrosion by oxide layer).
characters: Mama Wanjiru: a food seller in Mombasa who cooks ugali in an aluminium sufuria and asks why her pot is safe while chlorine in her tap water is poisonous as a gas. Mr. Otieno: the Grade 10 teacher at a school in Kisumu who performs the sodium demonstration behind a safety screen; he wears goggles and a lab coat, uses a pea-sized piece only, and keeps sodium in paraffin oil. Akinyi and Kiprop: two learners who keep the Driving Question Board (DQB) and the class family model; Akinyi is curious about why sodium is dangerous, Kiprop asks why street lamps glow yellow. Mombasa water works: treats drinking water with chlorine at about 0.5 mg/L. Thika Road street lamps: sodium vapour lamps glowing yellow-orange. Nairobi: also uses chlorine for water treatment; Nairobi also hosts the electric cable factory for copper wiring (use for Lesson 7 context). Kericho: tea region where mabati roofs are common in farm buildings. Jua kali artisans in Gikomba (Nairobi): make sufuria from recycled aluminium and use galvanised mabati sheets. Class DQB: a wall chart where learners post questions on sticky notes, sorted into 'Properties', 'Reactivity', 'Uses' and 'Safety'. Class Family Model: a large wall periodic table that learners annotate each lesson. Safety rules: goggles on, small quantities, never touch sodium with bare hands, no water near stored sodium, dispose of residues as directed by teacher.
outcome: Elements are chosen for jobs because of their properties, which depend on their atomic structure, especially the number of outer electrons, and so on their position in the periodic table. Sodium reacts violently with water because its single outer electron is lost very easily, but once combined with chlorine as NaCl (salt) it is stable and safe to eat; chlorine, a toxic gas in large amounts, kills disease-causing microbes at a tiny dose of about 0.5 mg/L in Mombasa water. Aluminium (light, heat-conducting, corrosion-resistant) suits the sufuria, copper (excellent conductor, ductile) suits wire, zinc coats iron for mabati, and unreactive noble gases such as neon suit signs, with sodium vapour used in Thika Road lamps for its yellow light. The periodic table lets us predict an element's family behaviour and so match element to job, balanced against safety, cost and availability.
conventions: Use 'element', 'compound', 'group' (vertical column) and 'period' (horizontal row). Family names: alkali metals (Group 1), alkaline earth metals (Group 2), halogens (Group 17), noble gases (Group 18), transition metals (the central block). Always use 'chemical family' for a group with similar properties. Use symbols Na, K, Li, Mg, Ca, Al, Fe, Cu, Zn, Pb, Cl, Ne, Ar, H. Chemical equations use '->' with state symbols optional: (s), (l), (g), (aq); balance atoms every time. 'Reactivity' means how readily an element loses or gains electrons to form compounds; metal reactivity rises with ease of losing outer electrons. Units: density in g/cm3, temperature in degrees Celsius (C), melting and boiling points in C, concentration in mg/L. Water density = 1.00 g/cm3. Sodium (not 'Soda') is the element; salt means NaCl; 'sodium light' means sodium vapour lamp. Use 'outer electron(s)' not 'valence electrons'. Do not introduce ionic bonding in detail, formulas of ions, or electronegativity; Lesson 4 introduces only the idea that the metal atom loses its outer electron(s). Teacher demonstrations only for sodium, potassium and lithium; learners do not handle them. Learners may handle Mg ribbon, Al, Cu, Fe, Zn samples with goggles. Phenomenon is referred to as 'the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle'. Teaching sequence uses five phases: Predict, Observe, Explain, DQB, Model Building.

lessonMap.focus: Anchoring phenomenon: Kenyan objects and the sodium demonstration
lessonMap.teaches: Different elements have very different properties (some dangerous alone) yet each is useful; students raise questions about why an element suits a job
lessonMap.buildsOn: No earlier lesson; builds on Grade 9 knowledge of elements and the periodic table only
lessonMap.usesData: Anchor objects list (sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, Mombasa water, Thika Road lamp) and the sodium-in-water demo

lessonMap.focus: Chemical families and the periodic table layout
lessonMap.teaches: Elements are grouped in the periodic table into families (alkali, alkaline earth, halogens, noble gases, transition metals) by position; group number links to similar behaviour
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 1: DQB questions and the list of objects' elements
lessonMap.usesData: First 20 elements table with symbols, Z and families; location of transition metals

lessonMap.teaches: How to compare physical properties (hardness, density, melting point, conductivity) and find patterns across and within families
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 2: family groupings used to organise the data table
lessonMap.usesData: Physical data table (density, melting point, hardness, conductivity)

lessonMap.teaches: Alkali metals are very reactive because each has one outer electron that is easily lost; reactivity increases down the group (Li < Na < K); safety and first aid for reactive metals
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 1: sodium demo; Lesson 2: Group 1 position; Lesson 3: soft, low density, low melting point
lessonMap.usesData: Alkali metal reactions with water, key equations for Na, Li, K, electron arrangements (Li 2,1; Na 2,8,1; K 2,8,8,1)

lessonMap.teaches: Alkaline earth metals have two outer electrons and are less reactive than alkali metals; how to compare reactivity by experiment (air, water, acid) and write balanced equations for Mg
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 4: reactivity and outer electrons, equation writing; Lesson 3: Mg is denser and higher melting than Na
lessonMap.usesData: Mg data (burns in air, no cold-water reaction, reacts with dilute HCl), equations 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO and Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2, reactivity order K > Na > Li > Ca > Mg

lessonMap.teaches: Halogens (7 outer electrons) are reactive non-metals, with chlorine used in small doses for water treatment; noble gases have full outer shells so are unreactive, which suits lighting and signs
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 4 and Lesson 5: outer electrons and reactivity; Lesson 1: Mombasa water and street lamp; Lesson 2: Group 17 and 18
lessonMap.usesData: Chlorine data (greenish-yellow gas, 0.5 mg/L), 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl, Ne and Ar electron arrangements, noble gas boiling points

lessonMap.teaches: Transition metals are strong, dense, good conductors with high melting points, so uses are matched to specific properties (and trade-offs such as toxicity of lead)
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 2: position of the transition block; Lesson 3: physical properties data; Lesson 1: copper wire and mabati
lessonMap.usesData: Fe, Cu, Zn, Pb, Al physical data and the uses list (wiring, mabati, galvanising, batteries, sufuria)

lessonMap.focus: Putting it together: choosing the right element for the job
lessonMap.teaches: Using evidence from properties, reactivity and periodic table position to justify choosing an element for a new Kenyan product, weighing safety, cost and availability
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 1-7: completed family model and DQB answers
lessonMap.usesData: All anchor data; final outcome linking sodium, chlorine, salt, aluminium, copper, zinc and noble gases
